title: Hoddeok
subtitle: Sweet filled pancakes with brown sugar and nuts
excerpt: Hoddeok are Korean street-food pancakes made from a yeasted dough filled with brown sugar, cinnamon, and sesame seeds. This recipe makes 8 pancakes and takes about 110 minutes including the dough rising time. The sugar melts inside the pancake as it fries, creating a warm, caramelised filling that oozes when cut.
sourceNotes: Hoddeok is thought to have been introduced to Korea by Chinese merchants during the late Joseon dynasty in the 19th century, who sold a filled pancake from street stalls. The dish was adapted with local ingredients and became firmly embedded in Korean street food culture. It is particularly associated with winter street markets and remains one of the most popular street foods sold at Korean outdoor food stalls today.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made up to the end of the first rise, then covered and refrigerated overnight. Bring to room temperature for 30 minutes before shaping.

glossaryTerms.definition: Hoddeok is a Korean street-food pancake made from a soft yeasted dough that is filled with a mixture of brown sugar, cinnamon, and crushed nuts, then fried flat in oil. As the pancake cooks, the sugar filling melts into a hot caramel. They are sold from street stalls in winter, eaten immediately while the caramel is still liquid inside.

Yeasted dough uses yeast as a leavening agent. The yeast feeds on sugars in the flour and releases carbon dioxide, causing the dough to expand and become light and airy. For a successful rise, the yeast needs warmth: the dough should be left in a warm, draught-free spot. A dough that doubles in size after an hour is ready. Under-risen dough produces dense, chewy results.

. The dough is soft and slightly sticky, filled with a mixture of brown sugar, cinnamon, and sesame seeds, and fried flat in oil until golden on both sides. The sugar inside melts into hot caramel during frying.

The dough for hoddeok is softer and wetter than bread dough. Do not add more flour to compensate for the stickiness: the moisture is what gives the pancake its characteristic soft, slightly chewy texture. Oil your hands before shaping each pancake rather than flouring them. Press the filled dough ball flat in the pan using the back of a spatula or a flat press, holding it down firmly for the first 30 seconds so it spreads into a round disc.

items.prepNote: about 40C, warm to the touch but not hot

content.text: Mix the flour, caster sugar, and instant yeast in a large bowl. Add the warm water and stir until a shaggy dough forms. Knead in the bowl for 3 to 4 minutes until smooth. The dough will be soft and slightly sticky. Cover with a clean cloth and leave in a warm spot to rise for 60 to 70 minutes until doubled in size.
While the dough rises, make the filling: mix together the brown sugar, cinnamon, and sesame seeds in a small bowl.
Once risen, punch the dough down gently. Oil your hands lightly. Divide the dough into 8 equal portions.

Take one portion and flatten it in your palm. Place a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre. Gather the edges of the dough up and around the filling and pinch firmly to seal. Roll gently into a ball. Repeat with the remaining portions.
Heat 1 to 2 tablespoons of oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Place 2 to 3 dough balls in the pan, sealed-side down, leaving space between them.
Immediately press each ball flat with the back of a spatula, spreading it to about 10cm in diameter. Hold the pressure for 20 seconds.
Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until the underside is golden. Flip carefully and cook for a further 2 minutes until the second side is golden and the filling is bubbling inside.
Remove to a plate and leave for 1 minute before eating. The filling will be extremely hot. Repeat with the remaining pancakes, adding oil to the pan as needed.

items.symptom: The dough has not risen after an hour
items.cause: The water was too hot and killed the yeast, or too cold and failed to activate it
items.fix: Water at 40C feels warm but not uncomfortable on the inside of your wrist. If the dough has not risen at all after 90 minutes, the yeast is likely dead. Start again with fresh yeast and water at the correct temperature

items.symptom: The filling leaks out during frying
items.cause: The dough was not sealed tightly enough around the filling
items.fix: Pinch the dough edges together firmly and check there are no gaps before placing the ball in the pan, sealed-side down. Press flat gently and evenly rather than in a single forceful press

items.symptom: The outside is golden but the dough in the centre is raw
items.cause: The heat was too high, browning the outside before the inside cooked
items.fix: Use medium rather than medium-high heat and allow 2 to 3 full minutes per side. The pancake should sizzle gently rather than spit aggressively

content.text: Hoddeok is winter street food in Korea. They are sold from stalls at outdoor markets and along shopping streets, handed over in small paper cups to protect fingers from the hot caramel inside. The smell of sugar and cinnamon in cold air is strongly associated with Korean winter in the same way that roasting chestnuts are in some European cities. At home they are a weekend treat, eaten warm from the pan with nothing alongside them. The hot liquid sugar inside is part of the pleasure and the hazard.
